name: Carla Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to you. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy packaging for Northgate Packaging, a distributor in the business park off the bypass. Cardboard boxes, tape, pallet wrap, padded mailers, the stuff online shops and small factories go through by the tonne. I start at half seven with an AI tool I set up myself that flags which lines will run out in the next fortnight, then I spend the day on the phone with paper mills and box makers arguing about prices that change every month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing things. Last winter the mill put prices up 12% overnight, and I found a smaller box maker two hours north who undercut them and saved us a fortune. What wears me out is the old-timers at Northgate who think a spreadsheet is witchcraft. My partner Rhys works in his family's haulage firm, and between his lorries and my boxes, our dinner conversation is very glamorous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: use the tools for what they're good at and stop expecting miracles. At church coffee I'd probably tell someone their teenager should learn a trade anyway. Online I'd share my reorder setup, because it still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My AI tool already saves me a day a week, and if AI stops there, I'm still the quickest buyer at Northgate. The job looks steady to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep improving my own tools, maybe build one to compare mill price lists. I'd ask for a pay rise in the summer and show them the money I saved on the box maker deal. I'd keep putting 300 a month away, because Rhys and I want to buy a house near his parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Nothing in that picture keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've put a lot into these tools. Would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tiny bit, yes. I was hoping the tools would get good enough to take the boring half of my job so I could do more of the deals. But it's a small disappointment, not a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you right now, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We've got about four months saved, rent is fair, and Rhys's family business is doing alright. The packaging trade goes up and down with online shopping, but people will always need boxes.

say: I'd tell people to use the tools for **what they're good at**, not miracles.
I'd share my **reorder setup** online, because it still works.
think: My tool already saves me **a day a week**, so I'm ahead.
The **job looks steady** in this world, and I'm the quickest buyer at Northgate.
do: Build a tool to compare **mill price lists**.
Ask for a **summer pay rise**, citing the box maker savings.
Save **300 a month** toward a house near Rhys's parents.
feel: **Comfortable**, with nothing in this picture keeping me up.
S0.quote: My AI tool already saves me a day a week, and if AI stops there, I'm still the quickest buyer at Northgate.
fieldNote: She's an **early adopter** who built her own tools, unusual for a traditional outlook.
Money feels **secure**: four months saved, fair rent, her partner's family firm doing well.
She's mildly **disappointed** the tools wouldn't free her for more deal-making.

steps.text: Build an AI tool to compare paper mill price lists
Ask for a summer pay rise citing the box maker deal
Save 300 a month toward a house near Rhys's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business and good for customers, and people who learn it will be fine. At work I'd offer to train anyone who wants it. I'd be honest that some roles will shrink, because pretending otherwise doesn't help anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it helps me. Buying is right on that list, but I'm the one who'd set the system up. Northgate will want one buyer who understands both the paper mills and the software, and I'm planning to be that buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my boss, Gordon, in the first month with a plan to automate our reorders properly, with me running it. I'd start a small online shop on the side selling packaging to craft sellers on weekends, since I know the suppliers. And I'd keep the 300 a month going, maybe 400 if the shop makes anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about the people it'll hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat in accounts payable, who's been there twenty years and still prints invoices. And Owen, a young buyer who's quite good on the phone but won't touch the new tools. I'd try to bring them along, but you can't make someone learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What's the risk to you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Northgate decides it needs no buyers at all, just the software and someone in head office. That's possible. But I'd have the shop and Rhys's family firm, so I wouldn't be starting from nothing.

say: I'd say it's **good for business** and people who learn it will be fine.
I'd be honest that **some roles shrink**, and offer to train anyone at work.
think: I'd be the one who **sets the system up**, so it likely helps me.
Northgate will want one buyer who knows **mills and software**, and I plan to be that buyer.
do: Pitch Gordon a plan to **automate reorders** with me running it.
Start a weekend **online shop** selling packaging to craft sellers.
Raise savings to **400 a month** if the shop earns.
feel: **Excited**, with some **guilt** about the colleagues it will hit.
S1.quote: Northgate will want one buyer who understands both the paper mills and the software, and I'm planning to be that buyer.
fieldNote: She expects to **keep her job** by running the automation, so her worry is for others.
She names **Pat and Owen** as colleagues likely to be left behind.
A **side shop** and her partner's family firm give her a fallback if the role disappears.

steps.text: Pitch Gordon a plan to automate Northgate's reorders with her in charge
Open a weekend online shop selling packaging to craft sellers
Raise savings to 400 a month if the shop earns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, and moaning won't stop it, so get moving. At church I'd tell people to look after their families and each other. Online I'd share what I was doing, because people need examples, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job is gone by 2028. If the AI can do any thinking work, it'll run Northgate's purchasing without me, probably better. The part I'm proud of, setting up the AI tools, is exactly what makes me easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Rhys's dad, Glyn, straight away about moving into the haulage firm's office, running their planning and pricing with AI before a bigger firm undercuts them. I'd cut back, sell my car and use Rhys's, and push our savings to six months. I'd keep the craft packaging shop going, since the customers like a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but busy. Like the morning of a big exam you've half prepared for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Rhys's family firm is lorries. Does the three-year gap before robots help your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a bit and hurts a bit. Rhys and the drivers are safe until robots come, about 2031, but the firm's office work gets hit in 2028 like mine. So we'd have three years to make the firm lean and smart before the lorries drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gordon when you hand in your notice, or when he hands you yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank Gordon, because he gave me a chance at 23. I'd tell him to keep someone who knows the mills by name, because the software won't get you a favour when the price jumps. Then I'd go and do the same for Glyn's firm.

say: I'd say it's happening and **moaning won't stop it**, so get moving.
At church I'd urge people to **look after their families** and each other.
think: Setting up the tools is exactly what makes me **easy to replace**.
do: Ask Glyn to let me run **the haulage firm's planning** and pricing.
Sell my car and grow savings to **six months**.
Keep the **craft packaging shop** running for extra income.
feel: **Nervous** but busy, like a big exam I've half prepared for.
S2.quote: The part I'm proud of, setting up the AI tools, is exactly what makes me easy to replace.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the buyer job** but has a concrete route into the family haulage firm.
The household faces a **two-step hit**: office work in 2028, Rhys's driving around 2031.
Her **faith and family** shape the answer: look after your own, don't wait for help.

steps.text: Move into Glyn's haulage office to run planning and pricing
Sell her car and share Rhys's
Grow savings from four to six months of costs
Keep the weekend craft packaging shop running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so there's no excuse not to. I'd push at work for Northgate to train people properly. With family I'd say save, and don't sign up for big debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the buying job goes in 2031 instead, when I'm 32. But five years is long enough to build something with Rhys's family that can stand up when the robots come for the lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stay at Northgate and start helping Glyn's firm one evening a week, setting up AI for route planning and quotes. I'd do a short course in transport management, about 900, so I'm not just the girlfriend who's good with computers. We'd put part of our savings into the firm's first electric lorry if Glyn agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. It gives me something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be dropped into the haulage firm in a hurry. With five years I can build the haulage firm's systems properly while I've still got my Northgate pay. By the time the AGI comes, the firm is already running on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for how this lands on people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly nobody, it's progress, like the lorry replacing the horse. But big firms will grab it first and squeeze small ones like Glyn's, and I'd want the government to stop that, not hand out money afterwards.

say: I'd say we have **time to get ready**, so there's no excuse.
I'd tell family to save and **avoid big debts**.
think: My buying job goes **in 2031**, when I'm 32.
Five years lets me build **something with Rhys's family** before robots reach the lorries.
do: Spend **one evening a week** setting up AI route planning for Glyn's firm.
Put savings into the firm's **first electric lorry**.
feel: **Anxious** in a useful way, with something to do with the worry.
S3.quote: With five years I can build the haulage firm's systems properly while I've still got my Northgate pay.
fieldNote: She still expects the **Northgate job to end**, but uses the time to build a family business.
She blames **no one** for progress, but wants government to stop big firms squeezing small ones.
She wants a **qualification** so the family sees her as more than good with computers.

steps.text: Set up AI route planning and quotes for Glyn's firm weekly
Take a transport management course costing about 900
Put part of their savings into the firm's first electric lorry

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd keep telling people at work to learn the tools. Online I'd share the steps I'm taking, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it suits me. I'd have time to move into Rhys's family firm properly and own part of it. The buyer job at Northgate still goes by 2036, but I'd have left for the family haulage firm before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few years I'd stay at Northgate and get promoted if I can, while helping the haulage firm on the side. Around year three, I'd join the firm full time and buy into it. We'd buy a house and probably start a family, because there's room to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There's a shadow, but I can see where I'm walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you worry you'd get comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Rhys says I could make a project out of boiling an egg, so I doubt it. If anything, I'd worry about rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself and Rhys by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully running a smaller, smarter haulage firm with self-driving lorries and a few people who know the customers. Maybe with a child or two, and Glyn retired on the profits. That's the dream, anyway.

say: I'd call ten years **a gift** to be used.
I'd keep sharing **practical steps** online and urge colleagues to keep learning the tools, without doom.
think: It **suits me**: time to move into Rhys's family firm properly.
The buying job goes by 2036, but **I'd have left** before then.
do: Stay at Northgate and **aim for promotion** in the first years.
Join the haulage firm **full time** and buy into it around year three.
Buy a **house** and probably start a family.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with a shadow but a clear path.
S4.quote: The buyer job at Northgate still goes by 2036, but I'd have left for the family haulage firm before then.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees a **planned exit**, not a loss, so her own income looks safe.
She still notes a **shadow**: the haulage firm faces robot lorries around 2039.
Family plans **go ahead**, because the timeline gives room to plan.

steps.text: Buy a share of Glyn's haulage firm around year three
Leave Northgate for the haulage firm full time
Buy a house with Rhys and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits my job and the haulage firm's office at the same time, with no room to build anything. What would help is cheap loans or tax breaks for small family firms to buy the new tools, so they don't get swallowed by the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd miss it. I would. I'll miss arguing with paper mills about the price of cardboard, and nobody's going to believe that.

headlineQuote: I'll miss arguing with paper mills about the price of cardboard, and nobody's going to believe that.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** packaging buyer at Northgate Packaging, living with Rhys, whose family runs a haulage firm.
She uses AI **every day** and built her own reorder tool.
She's calm in the plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, betting she'll **run the automation**.
In the AGI pictures she expects to lose the buyer job and moves into the **family firm**.
Traditional on family and faith, she wants **small firms** protected from being squeezed by big ones.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting her job and the haulage firm's office at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** or tax breaks for small family firms to buy the new tools.
